title: Τρώων πυρά
titleEn: Hector’s Assembly and the Trojan Fires — Iliad 8.469–565
part: Hector’s Assembly and the Trojan Fires (8.469–565)
about: Zeus answers Hera: at dawn she will see him destroy still more of the Argive host, and Hector will not stop until Achilles rises beside the ships over the dead Patroclus; he cares nothing for her anger, even if she went to the lowest limits of earth and sea. Hera says nothing, and the sun sinks into Oceanus, to the Trojans’ regret and the Achaeans’ relief. Hector holds an assembly on a clear patch of ground away from the ships, leaning on his eleven-cubit spear. He admits that night has saved the Achaeans, orders the horses fed and the town to send out cattle, wine, food and wood for fires that will burn until dawn, sets boys, old men and women to keep watch and burn fires, and promises to learn at daybreak whether Diomedes or he will carry off the other’s spoils. The Trojans cheer, do as he says and sacrifice, though the gods take no share, since Ilium has become hateful to them. The part ends on a simile of stars around the moon and the thousand fires on the plain, each with fifty men beside it, while the horses stand feeding and wait for Dawn.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς·
sentences.l: Her answering addressed cloud-gatherer Zeus:
sentences.i: In answer Zeus who gathers the clouds said to her:
sentences.n: A new paragraph: Zeus replies to Hera. The line is the formula for an answer to a woman: τὴν is the article used as a pronoun, ‘her’, ἀπαμειβόμενος is ‘answering’, and προσέφη is ‘addressed’. νεφεληγερέτα, ‘cloud-gatherer’ (νεφέλη ‘cloud’ + ἀγείρω ‘gather’), is a stock epithet of Zeus, translated every time, and it keeps the old nominative ending -α (Attic would end in -ης). The English is the same as for this line where it stands earlier in the poem.

sentences.t:
ἠοῦς δὴ καὶ μᾶλλον ὑπερμενέα Κρονίωνα
ὄψεαι, αἴ κ’ ἐθέλῃσθα, βοῶπις πότνια Ἥρη
ὀλλύντ’ Ἀργείων πουλὺν στρατὸν αἰχμητάων·
sentences.i: “At dawn, ox-eyed lady Hera, if you wish, you will see the son of Cronus, of surpassing strength, destroying a great host of Argive spearmen all the more;
sentences.n: Zeus names himself in the third person, as Κρονίωνα ‘son of Cronus’ with the epithet ὑπερμενέα ‘exceeding-strong’ (‘of surpassing strength’), the object of ὄψεαι and joined to the participle ὀλλύντ’ ‘destroying’. ἠοῦς is a genitive of time, ‘at dawn’. ὄψεαι is the uncontracted future of ὁράω, and αἴ κ’ ἐθέλῃσθα ‘if you wish’ has the old ending -σθα. βοῶπις ‘ox-eyed’ is usually taken to mean large, calm eyes; πότνια is ‘lady’. καὶ μᾶλλον ‘even more’ could go with ὑπερμενέα (‘still mightier’) or with the destroying; the English puts it on the destroying. πουλύν is πολύν, and αἰχμητάων the epic genitive plural of αἰχμητής ‘spearman’.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ πρὶν πολέμου ἀποπαύσεται ὄβριμος Ἕκτωρ
πρὶν ὄρθαι παρὰ ναῦφι ποδώκεα Πηλεΐωνα,
ἤματι τῷ ὅτ’ ἂν οἳ μὲν ἐπὶ πρύμνῃσι μάχωνται
στείνει ἐν αἰνοτάτῳ περὶ Πατρόκλοιο θανόντος·
sentences.l:
for not before from war will cease mighty Hector
before to rise up beside the ships the fleet-footed son of Peleus,
on that day when they at the sterns fight
in a most dread narrow place, about Patroclus dead;
sentences.i: for mighty Hector will not cease from the war until the fleet-footed son of Peleus rises beside the ships, on that day when they fight at the sterns in a most dreadful narrow place, over the dead Patroclus;
sentences.n: Zeus gives the reason (γάρ) and a deadline: πρὶν … πρίν is ‘not … until’, with ὄρθαι, the epic aorist middle infinitive of ὄρνυμι, ‘to rise up’. ἀποπαύσεται (future middle) takes the genitive πολέμου. ὄβριμος ‘mighty’ and ποδώκεα ‘fleet-footed’ are stock epithets, translated every time; ναῦφι has the ending -φι, ‘by the ships’. Πηλεΐωνα, ‘son of Peleus’, is a patronymic for Achilles, who is not named. ἤματι τῷ ὅτ’ ἂν … μάχωνται is ‘on that day when they fight’, οἳ μὲν ‘they’ being unspecified. ἐπὶ πρύμνῃσι is ‘at the sterns’ of the beached ships, στεῖνος a ‘narrow place’ (a crush of men), αἰνοτάτῳ the superlative of αἰνός ‘dread’, θανόντος ‘dead’ (aorist participle).

sentences.t: ὣς γὰρ θέσφατόν ἐστι·
sentences.l: for so it is god-declared;
sentences.i: for so it is decreed;
sentences.n: θέσφατον is ‘declared by a god’ (θεός + the root of φημί), a thing that has been decreed; the Odyssey has the same word. ὣς is ‘so’, pointing back to what Zeus has just said. ἐστι is the enclitic form of εἰμί, so it has no accent of its own. The short sentence is a pause before Zeus turns on Hera.

sentences.t:
σέθεν δ’ ἐγὼ οὐκ ἀλεγίζω
χωομένης,
sentences.l:
but of you I do not care
being incensed,
sentences.i: and I do not care about you in your anger,
sentences.n: σέθεν is the epic genitive of σύ, ‘of you’, and ἀλεγίζω ‘care for’ governs it (the same words as at 1.180); χωομένης is the feminine genitive participle of χώομαι ‘be incensed’, agreeing with σέθεν, so ‘you being incensed’ means Hera. The sentence goes on through line 483, and the unit stops at the comma because that is where the sense pauses.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ εἴ κε τὰ νείατα πείραθ’ ἵκηαι
γαίης καὶ πόντοιο, ἵν’ Ἰάπετός τε Κρόνος τε
ἥμενοι οὔτ’ αὐγῇς Ὑπερίονος Ἠελίοιο
τέρποντ’ οὔτ’ ἀνέμοισι, βαθὺς δέ τε Τάρταρος ἀμφίς·
sentences.l:
not even if you come to the lowest limits
of earth and sea, where Iapetus and Cronus
sitting, neither in the rays of the Sun Hyperion
take delight nor in winds, and deep Tartarus lies around;
sentences.i: not even if you come to the lowest limits of earth and sea, where Iapetus and Cronus sit and take delight neither in the rays of the Sun, Hyperion, nor in winds, and deep Tartarus lies around them;
sentences.n: οὐδ’ εἴ κε … ἵκηαι is ‘not even if you come’: ἵκηαι is a subjunctive of ἵκω with the old ending -ηαι, and κε (= ἄν) goes with εἰ. νείατα is ‘lowest, undermost’, πείραθ’ is πείρατα ‘limits’. ἵνα ‘where’ introduces the place where Iapetus and Cronus, two of the older gods, sit (ἥμενοι); they ‘take delight’ (τέρποντ’, for τέρπονται) in neither sunlight nor wind. αὐγῇς ‘rays’ is a genitive, ἀνέμοισι a dative plural in -οισι, and Ὑπερίονος Ἠελίοιο is ‘the Sun Hyperion’, as in the Odyssey. βαθὺς δέ τε Τάρταρος ἀμφίς is ‘and deep Tartarus lies all around’; ἀμφίς is an adverb.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἢν ἔνθ’ ἀφίκηαι ἀλωμένη, οὔ σευ ἔγωγε
σκυζομένης ἀλέγω, ἐπεὶ οὐ σέο κύντερον ἄλλο.
sentences.l:
not even if you come there wandering, of you I at least
being sullen take no heed, since not than you more dog-like is another thing.”
sentences.i: nor if you come there in your wandering will I, for my part, heed you in your sullenness, since there is nothing more shameless than you.”
sentences.n: The speech ends with the sharpest insult in it. οὐδ’ ἢν is ‘not even if’, ἀφίκηαι a subjunctive, and ἀλωμένη the participle of ἀλάομαι ‘wander’, agreeing with the ‘you’ (Hera). σευ is the genitive of σύ and σκυζομένης the feminine participle of σκύζομαι ‘be sullen, sulk’, so ‘you being sullen’; ἀλέγω is ‘take heed’. κύντερον is the comparative of κύων ‘dog’, ‘more dog-like’, which in Greek means more shameless; the Odyssey uses the word in the same way. σέο is the genitive of comparison, ‘than you’, and οὐ … ἄλλο ‘nothing else’.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, τὸν δ’ οὔ τι προσέφη λευκώλενος Ἥρη.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and him not at all addressed white-armed Hera.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and white-armed Hera said nothing at all to him.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. φάτο is an unaugmented aorist (= ἔφατο) and τὸν is the article used as a pronoun, ‘him’. οὔ τι is ‘not at all’, so the line says that Hera answered nothing to him. λευκώλενος ‘white-armed’ is the stock epithet of Hera.

sentences.t:
ἐν δ’ ἔπεσ’ Ὠκεανῷ λαμπρὸν φάος ἠελίοιο
ἕλκον νύκτα μέλαιναν ἐπὶ ζείδωρον ἄρουραν.
sentences.l:
And fell into Oceanus the bright light of the sun,
drawing black night over the grain-giving plough-land.
sentences.i: And the bright light of the sun fell into Oceanus, drawing dark night over the grain-giving plough-land.
sentences.n: The sun sets. ἐν … ἔπεσ’ is ἔπεσε with its preverb apart (tmesis), ‘fell into’, and Ὠκεανῷ is the dative of Oceanus, the great river that circles the earth. φάος ‘light’ is neuter, so ἕλκον ‘drawing’ is a neuter participle agreeing with it. μέλαιναν ‘black’ is here an epithet of night. ζείδωρον ἄρουραν is a stock phrase; ζείδωρος is usually taken as ‘grain-giving’ (ζειά ‘grain’ + δῶρον), with an ancient alternative ‘life-giving’, and ἄρουρα is ploughed land.

sentences.t:
Τρωσὶν μέν ῥ’ ἀέκουσιν ἔδυ φάος, αὐτὰρ Ἀχαιοῖς
ἀσπασίη τρίλλιστος ἐπήλυθε νὺξ ἐρεβεννή.
sentences.l:
To the Trojans, for their part, unwilling, set the light, but to the Achaeans
welcome, thrice-prayed-for, came on night, the murky one.
sentences.i: For the Trojans the light set against their will, but for the Achaeans night, murky and welcome, much prayed for, came on.
sentences.n: ἔδυ is the aorist of δύω ‘set, go down’, and Τρωσίν … ἀέκουσιν is ‘to the Trojans unwilling’. The contrast is μέν … αὐτάρ, ‘for the Trojans … but for the Achaeans’. ἀσπασίη is ‘welcome’; ἐπήλυθε is the aorist of ἐπέρχομαι ‘come on’. τρίλλιστος is ‘thrice-prayed-for’ (τρι- ‘three’ + the root of λίσσομαι ‘pray’), the usual explanation; the τρι- may only be intensive, ‘much prayed for’. ἐρεβεννή is ‘murky’, from Ἔρεβος ‘darkness’.

sentences.t:
Τρώων αὖτ’ ἀγορὴν ποιήσατο φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ
νόσφι νεῶν ἀγαγὼν ποταμῷ ἔπι δινήεντι,
ἐν καθαρῷ ὅθι δὴ νεκύων διεφαίνετο χῶρος.
sentences.l:
Of the Trojans in turn an assembly made glorious Hector,
apart from the ships having led them, by the eddying river,
in a clear place, where indeed of the dead showed through the ground.
sentences.i: Then glorious Hector held an assembly of the Trojans, leading them away from the ships to the eddying river, to a clear place where the ground showed through, free of the dead.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. Τρώων ἀγορήν is ‘an assembly of the Trojans’, ποιήσατο the aorist middle of ποιέω, ‘made for himself’, the idiom for holding an assembly; αὖτε is ‘then, in turn’. φαίδιμος ‘glorious’ is Hector’s stock epithet, translated every time. νόσφι νεῶν is ‘apart from the ships’; ἀγαγών ‘having led’ them. ἔπι is ἐπί placed after its noun (hence the accent on the first syllable), and δινήεντι is ‘eddying’, from δίνη ‘eddy’. ἐν καθαρῷ is ‘in a clear place’; νεκύων διεφαίνετο χῶρος is ‘the ground showed through of the dead’. The usual explanation is ‘showed through, clear of corpses’; the genitive could instead mean ‘among the dead’.

sentences.t:
ἐξ ἵππων δ’ ἀποβάντες ἐπὶ χθόνα μῦθον ἄκουον
τόν ῥ’ Ἕκτωρ ἀγόρευε Διῒ φίλος·
sentences.l:
and from their horses having stepped down, to the ground they listened to the speech
which Hector was declaring, dear to Zeus;
sentences.i: They stepped down from their horses to the ground and listened to the speech that Hector, dear to Zeus, was declaring;
sentences.n: ἐξ ἵππων ἀποβάντες is ‘having stepped down from the horses’, the aorist participle of ἀποβαίνω; the horses are the chariot-teams. ἄκουον is an imperfect, ‘they were listening’, and μῦθον is the ‘speech’ of the next lines. τόν ῥ’ is τὸν ἄρα with the article used as a relative, ‘which’; ἀγόρευε is ‘was declaring’. Διῒ φίλος ‘dear to Zeus’ is a stock epithet, translated every time; Διῒ is printed with a diaeresis, as the edition has it. The unit ends mid-line, at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ἐν δ’ ἄρα χειρὶ
ἔγχος ἔχ’ ἑνδεκάπηχυ·
sentences.l:
and in his hand
a spear he held, eleven-cubit;
sentences.i: and in his hand he held a spear eleven cubits long;
sentences.n: ἐν is an adverb here, ‘in’ (his hand), and ἔχ’ is ἔχε, ‘he held’, an imperfect. ἑνδεκάπηχυ, ‘eleven-cubit’ (ἕνδεκα + πῆχυς ‘cubit’, the forearm), agrees with ἔγχος ‘spear’; a cubit’s length is not fixed. The unit begins in the middle of 8.493, after the previous stop.

sentences.t:
πάροιθε δὲ λάμπετο δουρὸς
αἰχμὴ χαλκείη, περὶ δὲ χρύσεος θέε πόρκης,
τῷ ὅ γ’ ἐρεισάμενος ἔπεα Τρώεσσι μετηύδα·
sentences.l:
and in front gleamed of the spear
the point, bronze, and around it ran a golden ring,
on it leaning he among the Trojans spoke words:
sentences.i: and the bronze point of the spear gleamed in front, and a golden ring ran round it, and leaning on it he spoke words among the Trojans:
sentences.n: Lines 494b–495 stand in an earlier part of the poem (6.319–320); their English is reused here, with a comma where this sentence goes on. πάροιθε is ‘in front’, λάμπετο ‘gleamed’, αἰχμή the ‘point’ of the spear (δουρός), χαλκείη ‘of bronze’; περὶ … θέε is ‘ran around’ (περί as an adverb, θέω ‘run’), and πόρκης is a ‘ring’ round the spear-head, the sense usually understood. In 496, τῷ ‘on it’ is the article used as a pronoun, for the spear, ὅ γ’ is ‘he’, and ἐρεισάμενος, the aorist middle participle of ἐρείδω, is ‘leaning’. μετηύδα is ‘spoke among’, the verb for addressing a group. The unit runs across three lines because the sentence does.

sentences.t: κέκλυτέ μευ Τρῶες καὶ Δάρδανοι ἠδ’ ἐπίκουροι·
sentences.l: “Hear me, Trojans and Dardanians and allies;
sentences.i: “Hear me, Trojans, Dardanians and allies;
sentences.n: Hector’s speech begins and runs to 541. κέκλυτε is the perfect imperative of κλύω, ‘hear’, the usual opening for a call to attention, and μευ is the epic genitive of ἐγώ. Δάρδανοι, the Dardanians, are the Trojans under another of their names; ἐπίκουροι are ‘allies’, the troops from elsewhere. The English is that of the same line elsewhere in the poem.

sentences.t:
νῦν ἐφάμην νῆάς τ’ ὀλέσας καὶ πάντας Ἀχαιοὺς
ἂψ ἀπονοστήσειν προτὶ Ἴλιον ἠνεμόεσσαν·
sentences.l:
Now I said, the ships having destroyed and all the Achaeans,
back to return to windy Ilios;
sentences.i: Just now I thought that, once I had destroyed the ships and all the Achaeans, I would go back home to windy Ilios;
sentences.n: νῦν ἐφάμην is ‘just now I said (to myself)’, and the verb takes a future infinitive, ἀπονοστήσειν ‘to return home’ (νόστος ‘homecoming’), with ἂψ ‘back’. ὀλέσας is the aorist participle of ὄλλυμι ‘destroy’, ‘having destroyed’, and its subject is the speaker; the Achaeans are πάντας Ἀχαιούς ‘all the Achaeans’. προτί is πρός ‘to’. Ἴλιον ἠνεμόεσσαν has the stock epithet ‘windy’ (ἠνεμόεις, from ἄνεμος ‘wind’); Ἴλιον is accusative, ‘Ilios’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ πρὶν κνέφας ἦλθε, τὸ νῦν ἐσάωσε μάλιστα
Ἀργείους καὶ νῆας ἐπὶ ῥηγμῖνι θαλάσσης.
sentences.l:
but earlier darkness came, which now has saved most of all
the Argives and the ships on the surf-line of the sea.
sentences.i: but darkness came before that, and it is that which has now saved, most of all, the Argives and their ships on the shore where the sea breaks.
sentences.n: ἀλλά ‘but’ turns from the hope to the fact. πρίν is an adverb here, ‘before, earlier’, so πρὶν κνέφας ἦλθε is ‘but earlier darkness came’, that is, before the Trojan hope could come true. τό is the article used as a relative pronoun, ‘which’, and picks up the darkness; ἐσάωσε is the aorist of σαόω ‘save’, and μάλιστα ‘most of all’. Ἀργείους is the Argives, one of the poem’s three names for the army. ῥηγμῖνι is the dative of ῥηγμίν, ‘the place where the sea breaks’, the line of surf.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἤτοι νῦν μὲν πειθώμεθα νυκτὶ μελαίνῃ
δόρπά τ’ ἐφοπλισόμεσθα·
sentences.l:
But truly now let us obey black night
and make ready our suppers;
sentences.i: But for now let us give way to dark night and make ready our suppers;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἤτοι is ‘but truly’ (the edition prints ἤτοι as one word). πειθώμεθα is a subjunctive of πείθομαι ‘obey’, taking the dative νυκτὶ μελαίνῃ; ‘let us’ is its force, and so for ἐφοπλισόμεσθα, ‘let us make ready’, a short-vowel subjunctive. δόρπα is ‘suppers’, the plural of δόρπον. The line and the English are those of the same words elsewhere in the poem.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ καλλίτριχας ἵππους
λύσαθ’ ὑπὲξ ὀχέων, παρὰ δέ σφισι βάλλετ’ ἐδωδήν·
sentences.l:
but the fair-maned horses
unyoke from beneath the chariots, and beside them put food;
sentences.i: but unyoke the fair-maned horses from the chariots and set food beside them;
sentences.n: ἀτάρ is ‘but, and’. λύσαθ’ is λύσατε (the τ becomes θ before the rough breathing of ὑπέξ), the aorist active imperative of λύω, ‘unyoke’, and ὑπὲξ ὀχέων is ‘out from under the chariots’ (ὄχεα). καλλίτριχας, ‘fair-maned’ (κάλλος + θρίξ), is a stock epithet of horses, translated every time. παρὰ … βάλλετ’ is tmesis, ‘put beside’, and σφισι is ‘for them’, the horses. ἐδωδήν is ‘food’, here fodder.

sentences.t:
ἐκ πόλιος δ’ ἄξεσθε βόας καὶ ἴφια μῆλα
καρπαλίμως, οἶνον δὲ μελίφρονα οἰνίζεσθε
σῖτόν τ’ ἐκ μεγάρων, ἐπὶ δὲ ξύλα πολλὰ λέγεσθε,
sentences.l:
and from the city bring cattle and stout flocks
swiftly, and honey-hearted wine get for yourselves
and food from the halls, and wood in plenty gather,
sentences.i: and bring cattle and stout flocks from the city, swiftly, and get yourselves heart-sweetening wine and food from the halls, and gather wood in plenty as well,
sentences.n: A run of plural imperatives: ἄξεσθε ‘bring (for yourselves)’, οἰνίζεσθε ‘get yourselves wine’ (a verb made from οἶνος), and λέγεσθε ‘gather’, with ἐπί … λέγεσθε split by tmesis, ‘gather in addition’. ἴφια μῆλα, ‘stout flocks’, is a stock phrase for sheep and goats; μελίφρονα ‘honey-hearted’ (the English ‘heart-sweetening’) is a stock epithet of wine whose sense is not certain. καρπαλίμως is ‘swiftly’. σῖτον is food, and μεγάρων is ‘halls’. The sentence goes on for four more lines, and this unit stops at the comma after the three orders.

sentences.t:
ὥς κεν παννύχιοι μέσφ’ ἠοῦς ἠριγενείης
καίωμεν πυρὰ πολλά, σέλας δ’ εἰς οὐρανὸν ἵκῃ,
μή πως καὶ διὰ νύκτα κάρη κομόωντες Ἀχαιοὶ
φεύγειν ὁρμήσωνται ἐπ’ εὐρέα νῶτα θαλάσσης.
sentences.l:
so that all night long until early-born dawn
we may burn many fires, and the blaze to heaven may come,
lest in some way even through the night the long-haired-of-head Achaeans
set out to flee over the broad back of the sea.
sentences.i: so that we may keep many fires burning all night long until early-born dawn, and the blaze may reach heaven, lest in some way even in the night the long-haired Achaeans set out to flee over the sea’s broad back.
sentences.n: ὥς κεν … καίωμεν is a purpose clause, ‘so that we may burn’ (a subjunctive with κεν), and σέλας ‘blaze’ is the subject of ἵκῃ ‘may come to’. παννύχιοι is ‘all night long’, and ἠοῦς ἠριγενείης ‘early-born dawn’ uses the stock epithet of Dawn, translated every time. μή πως … ὁρμήσωνται is a fear clause: ‘lest in some way they set out’. κάρη κομόωντες, ‘long-haired’ (literally wearing the hair long on the head), is the stock epithet of the Achaeans. ἐπ’ εὐρέα νῶτα θαλάσσης is the stock phrase ‘over the broad back of the sea’, and εὐρέα is the neuter plural of εὐρύς ‘broad’.

sentences.t: μὴ μὰν ἀσπουδί γε νεῶν ἐπιβαῖεν ἕκηλοι,
sentences.l: let them not, truly, without trouble go aboard their ships at ease,
sentences.i: Let them not board their ships at ease, without trouble,
sentences.n: μὴ μάν is ‘surely not’, and ἐπιβαῖεν is an aorist optative used as a prohibition, ‘let them not go aboard’, with the genitive νεῶν. ἀσπουδί is ‘without exertion, without trouble’, from ἀ- + σπουδή; the sense here follows the context. ἕκηλοι is ‘at ease’, nominative plural agreeing with the Achaeans. The sentence continues in the next unit, and this one ends at the comma.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὥς τις τούτων γε βέλος καὶ οἴκοθι πέσσῃ
βλήμενος ἢ ἰῷ ἢ ἔγχεϊ ὀξυόεντι
νηὸς ἐπιθρῴσκων, ἵνα τις στυγέῃσι καὶ ἄλλος
Τρωσὶν ἐφ’ ἱπποδάμοισι φέρειν πολύδακρυν Ἄρηα.
sentences.l:
but so that someone of them even at home may digest a missile,
having been struck by an arrow or by a sharp spear
leaping upon a ship, so that another too may hate
to bring against the horse-taming Trojans tearful Ares.
sentences.i: but so that one of them at least may have a missile to nurse even at home, struck by an arrow or a sharp spear as he leaps upon a ship, so that another too may hate to bring tearful battle against the Trojans, tamers of horses.
sentences.n: ὥς τις … πέσσῃ is a purpose clause, ‘so that some man … may digest’, its main verb left out: the sense is ‘(let them not go aboard at ease) but so that …’. βέλος πέσσῃ, literally ‘digest (cook) a missile’, is an idiom for suffering from a wound; ‘nurse’ gives the usual explanation. βλήμενος is an aorist middle participle of βάλλω with passive sense, ‘struck’; ἰῷ is the dative of ἰός ‘arrow’, ἔγχεϊ ὀξυόεντι ‘a sharp spear’, νηὸς ἐπιθρῴσκων ‘leaping upon a ship’. ἵνα τις στυγέῃσι is ‘so that someone may hate’. ἱπποδάμοισι is the stock epithet of the Trojans, and πολύδακρυν Ἄρηα ‘tearful Ares’ is war, the god’s name for battle.

sentences.t:
κήρυκες δ’ ἀνὰ ἄστυ Διῒ φίλοι ἀγγελλόντων
παῖδας πρωθήβας πολιοκροτάφους τε γέροντας
λέξασθαι περὶ ἄστυ θεοδμήτων ἐπὶ πύργων·
sentences.i: And let the heralds, dear to Zeus, announce through the town that boys in their first youth and old men grey at the temples are to lie down round the town on the god-built towers;
sentences.n: κήρυκες are ‘heralds’, and Διῒ φίλοι ‘dear to Zeus’ is the epithet that Hector had at 493; ἀγγελλόντων is a third-person plural imperative, ‘let them announce’. The announcement is in indirect form, with an infinitive: λέξασθαι, the aorist middle of λέγω in its sense ‘lay oneself down’, so to take up quarters for the night on the towers. πρωθήβας is ‘in first youth’ (πρῶτος + ἥβη), and πολιοκροτάφους ‘grey-templed’. θεοδμήτων is ‘god-built’; the walls and towers are the work of gods. ἄστυ is ‘town’.

sentences.t:
θηλύτεραι δὲ γυναῖκες ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν ἑκάστη
πῦρ μέγα καιόντων·
sentences.l:
and the female women in the halls, each one,
a great fire let them burn;
sentences.i: and let the womenfolk in the halls, each one, burn a great fire;
sentences.n: θηλύτεραι is the comparative of θῆλυς ‘female’, but without any comparison in sense, so it is ‘the women’, the female part of the household; the English ‘womenfolk’ gives the force. ἑκάστη ‘each (woman)’ is singular beside the plural subject. καιόντων is another third-person plural imperative, ‘let them burn’, with πῦρ μέγα ‘a great fire’. μεγάροισιν is the dative plural of μέγαρον ‘hall’. The unit ends mid-line, at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
φυλακὴ δέ τις ἔμπεδος ἔστω
μὴ λόχος εἰσέλθῃσι πόλιν λαῶν ἀπεόντων.
sentences.l:
and let a watch be, a firm one,
lest an ambush enter the city, the people being away.
sentences.i: and let there be a firm watch, lest an ambush enter the city while the people are away.
sentences.n: φυλακὴ δέ τις ἔμπεδος ἔστω is ‘let there be a watch, a firm one’: ἔμπεδος is ‘firm, unbroken’ and τις only softens it. μὴ … εἰσέλθῃσι is a fear clause with a subjunctive, ‘lest it enter’. λόχος is an ‘ambush’, a band lying in wait, and λαῶν ἀπεόντων is a genitive absolute, ‘the people being away’ (ἄπειμι), the fighting men outside the walls.

sentences.t: ὧδ’ ἔστω Τρῶες μεγαλήτορες ὡς ἀγορεύω·
sentences.l: Thus let it be, great-spirited Trojans, as I declare;
sentences.i: Let it be so, great-spirited Trojans, as I declare;
sentences.n: ὧδ’ is ‘thus’ and ἔστω ‘let it be’, a third-person imperative of εἰμί. μεγαλήτορες, ‘great-spirited’ (μέγας + ἦτορ ‘heart’), is a stock epithet of the Trojans here, translated every time; ὡς ἀγορεύω is ‘as I declare’.

sentences.t:
μῦθος δ’ ὃς μὲν νῦν ὑγιὴς εἰρημένος ἔστω,
τὸν δ’ ἠοῦς Τρώεσσι μεθ’ ἱπποδάμοις ἀγορεύσω.
sentences.l:
And the word that now, sound, has been spoken, let it be,
but that other at dawn among the horse-taming Trojans I shall declare.
sentences.i: Let this word, which has now been spoken, stand as sound; the other I shall declare at dawn among the Trojans, tamers of horses.
sentences.n: μῦθος is a ‘word’ or ‘speech’. ὑγιής is ‘sound’, and εἰρημένος the perfect passive participle of ἐρέω, ‘spoken’; ἔστω is again the imperative, ‘let it be’. μέν … δέ sets the word now spoken against another, τὸν δ’, which Hector will declare at dawn; ‘the other’ is the English for this contrast. The Greek does not say what the second word is. ἠοῦς is the genitive ‘at dawn’, and μεθ’ ἱπποδάμοις is ‘among the horse-taming’; ἀγορεύσω is a future.

sentences.t:
ἔλπομαι εὐχόμενος Διί τ’ ἄλλοισίν τε θεοῖσιν
ἐξελάαν ἐνθένδε κύνας κηρεσσιφορήτους,
οὓς κῆρες φορέουσι μελαινάων ἐπὶ νηῶν.
sentences.l:
I hope, praying to Zeus and to the other gods,
to drive out from here dogs borne by the death-fates,
whom the death-fates carry on black ships.
sentences.i: I hope, in prayer to Zeus and the other gods, to drive out from here dogs borne by the fates of death, whom the fates of death carry on black ships.
sentences.n: ἔλπομαι is ‘I hope’ (it can also be ‘expect’), and εὐχόμενος ‘praying’. Διί τ’ ἄλλοισίν τε θεοῖσιν is ‘to Zeus and to the other gods’. ἐξελάαν is the epic infinitive of ἐξελαύνω, ‘to drive out’. The ‘dogs’ are the Achaeans, who are insulted as the invaders that come on black ships (μελαινάων is the epic genitive plural). κηρεσσιφορήτους is a rare word, ‘borne by the death-fates’ (κῆρες + φέρω); its sense is not certain, and the line after it uses κῆρες φορέουσι for the same idea. A κήρ is a fate of death.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἤτοι ἐπὶ νυκτὶ φυλάξομεν ἡμέας αὐτούς,
πρῶϊ δ’ ὑπηοῖοι σὺν τεύχεσι θωρηχθέντες
νηυσὶν ἔπι γλαφυρῇσιν ἐγείρομεν ὀξὺν Ἄρηα.
sentences.l:
But truly for the night we shall guard ourselves,
and early in the morning, at dawn, in our armour armed,
at the hollow ships we shall rouse sharp Ares.
sentences.i: But for the night we shall keep guard over ourselves, and early in the morning, at daybreak, armed in our armour, we shall rouse keen battle at the hollow ships.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἤτοι is ‘but truly’. ἐπὶ νυκτί is ‘for the night’, and φυλάξομεν ἡμέας αὐτούς ‘we shall guard ourselves’ (ἡμέας = ἡμᾶς). πρῶϊ is ‘early in the morning’ and ὑπηοῖοι ‘at dawn’ (ὑπό + ἠώς); θωρηχθέντες is the aorist passive participle of θωρήσσω ‘arm’, ‘having armed ourselves’, σὺν τεύχεσι ‘with our armour’. ἐγείρομεν is a short-vowel subjunctive used for the future, ‘we shall rouse’. ὀξὺν Ἄρηα, ‘sharp Ares’, is battle, with the god’s name standing for war. νηυσὶν … γλαφυρῇσιν, ‘hollow ships’, is a stock phrase.

sentences.t:
εἴσομαι εἴ κέ μ’ ὁ Τυδεΐδης κρατερὸς Διομήδης
πὰρ νηῶν πρὸς τεῖχος ἀπώσεται, ἤ κεν ἐγὼ τὸν
χαλκῷ δῃώσας ἔναρα βροτόεντα φέρωμαι.
sentences.l:
I shall know whether the Tydeus’-son, strong Diomedes,
from beside the ships to the wall will thrust me away, or whether I him
with bronze having slain the bloody spoils may bear off.
sentences.i: I shall find out whether the son of Tydeus, strong Diomedes, will thrust me back from the ships to the wall, or whether I, having slain him with bronze, shall bear off his bloody spoils.
sentences.n: εἴσομαι is the future of οἶδα, ‘I shall know’, and εἴ κε … ἤ κεν sets two possibilities: ‘whether … or whether’. Τυδεΐδης, ‘son of Tydeus’, is a patronymic standing for Diomedes, who is named as well; κρατερός ‘strong’ is his stock epithet. ἀπώσεται is the future middle of ἀπωθέω ‘thrust away’, πὰρ νηῶν is ‘from beside the ships’ (πάρ = παρά), and πρὸς τεῖχος ‘to the wall’. ἐγὼ τὸν χαλκῷ δῃώσας is ‘I having slain him with bronze’; δῃώσας is the aorist participle of δηϊόω. ἔναρα are spoils stripped from a slain man, βροτόεντα ‘bloody’, and φέρωμαι the subjunctive middle, ‘bear off for myself’.

sentences.t:
αὔριον ἣν ἀρετὴν διαείσεται, εἴ κ’ ἐμὸν ἔγχος
μείνῃ ἐπερχόμενον·
sentences.l:
Tomorrow his own excellence he will see through, if my spear
he awaits as it comes on;
sentences.i: Tomorrow he will learn his own excellence, if he stands his ground against my spear as it comes on;
sentences.n: ἣν ἀρετήν has the possessive ὅς, ἥ, ὅν (‘his own’), not the relative; ἀρετή is ‘excellence’, here fighting prowess. διαείσεται is a rare word, usually explained as ‘will see through’, that is, find out or learn for himself; the exact sense is not certain. εἴ κ’ is εἰ κε, and μείνῃ the aorist subjunctive of μένω, ‘awaits, stands against’, with ἐμὸν ἔγχος ‘my spear’ as its object and ἐπερχόμενον ‘coming on’ agreeing with it. The unit ends mid-line, at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἐν πρώτοισιν ὀΐω
κείσεται οὐτηθείς, πολέες δ’ ἀμφ’ αὐτὸν ἑταῖροι
ἠελίου ἀνιόντος ἐς αὔριον·
sentences.i: but I think he will lie among the foremost, stabbed, and many of his companions around him, when tomorrow’s sun rises;
sentences.n: ὀΐω is ‘I think’, parenthetical, and ἐν πρώτοισιν ‘among the foremost’. κείσεται is the future of κεῖμαι ‘lie’, and οὐτηθείς the aorist passive participle of οὐτάω ‘stab’, a thrust from close at hand. πολέες is the epic form of πολλοί, ‘many’, with ἑταῖροι ‘companions’. ἠελίου ἀνιόντος is a genitive absolute, ‘the sun rising’, and ἐς αὔριον ‘on the morrow’. The unit begins in the middle of 8.536, after the previous ano teleia.

sentences.t:
εἰ γὰρ ἐγὼν ὣς
εἴην ἀθάνατος καὶ ἀγήρως ἤματα πάντα,
τιοίμην δ’ ὡς τίετ’ Ἀθηναίη καὶ Ἀπόλλων,
ὡς νῦν ἡμέρη ἥδε κακὸν φέρει Ἀργείοισιν.
sentences.l:
if only I, so surely,
were immortal and ageless for all my days,
and were honoured as Athena and Apollo are honoured,
as surely this day brings evil to the Argives.”
sentences.i: If only I were immortal and ageless for all my days, and honoured as Athena and Apollo are honoured, as surely as this day brings evil to the Argives.”
sentences.n: The speech ends in a wish that works like an oath. εἰ γάρ with the optative εἴην is ‘if only I were’; ἐγών is ἐγώ before a vowel. ὣς … ὡς is ‘as surely … as’: Hector would be immortal as surely as the day brings evil. ἀθάνατος ‘immortal’ and ἀγήρως ‘ageless’ go with ἤματα πάντα, ‘for all my days’. τιοίμην (an optative, ‘and I were honoured’) and τίετ’ (= τίεται, ‘is honoured’) are middle or passive forms of τίω ‘honour’. κακὸν φέρει Ἀργείοισιν is ‘brings evil to the Argives’. The unit begins in the middle of 8.538, after the ano teleia.

sentences.t: ὣς Ἕκτωρ ἀγόρευ’, ἐπὶ δὲ Τρῶες κελάδησαν.
sentences.l: So Hector declared, and upon it the Trojans cried aloud.
sentences.i: So Hector declared, and at that the Trojans cried aloud.
sentences.n: A new paragraph; the speech is over. ἀγόρευ’ is the imperfect ἀγόρευε, ‘was declaring’, with the elision mark. ἐπὶ … κελάδησαν is ἐπί used as an adverb, ‘thereupon’, with the aorist of κελαδέω ‘make a loud noise, cry out’; from the context the cry is assent.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἵππους μὲν λῦσαν ὑπὸ ζυγοῦ ἱδρώοντας,
δῆσαν δ’ ἱμάντεσσι παρ’ ἅρμασιν οἷσιν ἕκαστος·
sentences.l:
And they the horses, for their part, unyoked from under the yoke, sweating,
and tied them with straps beside their chariots, each man his own;
sentences.i: They unyoked the sweating horses from the yoke, and each man tied his horses with straps beside his own chariot;
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ is ‘and they’, the Trojans, and μέν … δέ sets the unyoking against the tying. λῦσαν is an aorist of λύω, with ὑπὸ ζυγοῦ ‘from under the yoke’. ἱδρώοντας is ‘sweating’ (ἱδρόω). δῆσαν is the aorist of δέω ‘tie’, ἱμάντεσσι ‘with straps’ (dative in -εσσι), and παρ’ ἅρμασιν ‘beside the chariots’. οἷσιν is the possessive ‘their own’ (= ἑοῖσιν), and ἕκαστος ‘each man’. This carries out Hector’s order of 503–504.

sentences.t:
ἐκ πόλιος δ’ ἄξοντο βόας καὶ ἴφια μῆλα
καρπαλίμως, οἶνον δὲ μελίφρονα οἰνίζοντο,
σῖτόν τ’ ἐκ μεγάρων, ἐπὶ δὲ ξύλα πολλὰ λέγοντο.
sentences.l:
and from the city they brought cattle and stout flocks
swiftly, and honey-hearted wine they got for themselves
and food from the halls, and wood in plenty they gathered.
sentences.i: and they brought cattle and stout flocks from the city, swiftly, and got themselves heart-sweetening wine and food from the halls, and gathered wood in plenty as well.
sentences.n: The same three tasks as Hector’s orders at 505–507, now done: ἄξοντο ‘brought for themselves’ (an aorist middle without augment), οἰνίζοντο ‘were getting themselves wine’, and λέγοντο ‘were gathering’, with ἐπὶ … λέγοντο split by tmesis. The stock phrases ἴφια μῆλα ‘stout flocks’ and μελίφρονα ‘honey-hearted’ (sense uncertain) are translated as before.

sentences.t:
[ἔρδον δ’ ἀθανάτοισι τεληέσσας ἑκατόμβας]
κνίσην δ’ ἐκ πεδίου ἄνεμοι φέρον οὐρανὸν εἴσω.
[ἡδεῖαν·
sentences.l:
[and they offered to the immortals complete hecatombs]
and the savour from the plain the winds bore into heaven,
[sweet one:
sentences.i: They sacrificed complete hecatombs to the immortals, and the winds bore the sweet savour up from the plain into heaven;
sentences.n: Square brackets, which the edition prints round 8.548 and 8.550–552, mean that its editors regard those lines as probably not original (athetized); the archive keeps them, so the brackets open here at 548 and again at 550. ἔρδον is the imperfect of ἔρδω ‘do’, which with a sacrifice means ‘offer’ (as at 1.315); the English ‘sacrificed’ gives the sense. τεληέσσας ‘complete’ describes hecatombs ‘brought to completion’. κνίσην is ‘savour’, the smell of the burning fat; ἄνεμοι φέρον is ‘the winds bore’, with οὐρανὸν εἴσω ‘into heaven’. ἡδεῖαν ‘sweet’ agrees with κνίσην and begins 550, after the stop that ends 549; the English moves it to the savour and leaves the brackets out.

sentences.t:
τῆς δ’ οὔ τι θεοὶ μάκαρες δατέοντο,]
[οὐδ’ ἔθελον·
sentences.l:
but of it the blessed gods had no share at all,]
[nor did they wish;
sentences.i: but the blessed gods took no share of it, and did not wish to;
sentences.n: The brackets close here at the end of 550 and open again at the start of 551 (see the note on the previous unit). τῆς is ‘of it’, the savour, a partitive genitive; δατέοντο is the imperfect of δατέομαι ‘divide among themselves’, with οὔ τι ‘not at all’. μάκαρες θεοί ‘blessed gods’ is a stock phrase. οὐδ’ ἔθελον is ‘nor did they wish’ (an imperfect, unaugmented in form).

sentences.t:
μάλα γάρ σφιν ἀπήχθετο Ἴλιος ἱρή,]
[καὶ Πρίαμος καὶ λαὸς ἐϋμμελίω Πριάμοιο]
οἳ δὲ μέγα φρονέοντες ἐπὶ πτολέμοιο γεφύρας
εἴατο παννύχιοι, πυρὰ δέ σφισι καίετο πολλά.
sentences.l:
for very much to them was hateful sacred Ilium,]
[and Priam and the people of Priam of the good ash-spear]
but they, thinking great things, on the bridges of war
sat all night long, and fires for them were burning, many.
sentences.i: for sacred Ilium was very hateful to them, and Priam, and the people of Priam of the good ash-spear; but they, with high thoughts, sat all night long on the bridges of war, and many fires burned for them.
sentences.n: The brackets stand round 551 and 552 and close at the end of 552; the edition prints no stop there, so this unit runs on into 553–554, where a new paragraph begins (not marked here, because the unit starts before it). σφιν is ‘to them’, the gods; ἀπήχθετο is the aorist of ἀπεχθάνομαι ‘become hateful to’, which takes the house word ‘was hateful’. The line καὶ Πρίαμος … Πριάμοιο (552) is 4.47 and has the same English. οἳ δέ is ‘but they’, the Trojans; μέγα φρονέοντες ‘thinking great things’; πτολέμοιο is πολέμοιο with an epic τ, and ‘the bridges of war’ is a phrase of unknown meaning (see 8.378); εἴατο ‘sat’.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἐν οὐρανῷ ἄστρα φαεινὴν ἀμφὶ σελήνην
φαίνετ’ ἀριπρεπέα, ὅτε τ’ ἔπλετο νήνεμος αἰθήρ·
sentences.l:
And as when in heaven the stars around the shining moon
appear outstanding, when the aether has become windless;
sentences.i: And as when in heaven the stars around the shining moon appear outstanding, when the upper air has become windless;
sentences.n: A simile begins: ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ is ‘and as when’. φαίνετ’ is φαίνεται ‘appear’; ἀριπρεπέα, ‘outstanding’, from ἀρι- (very) and πρέπω ‘be conspicuous’, agrees with ἄστρα. ὅτε τ’ ἔπλετο is ‘when it has become’, a general statement, and νήνεμος is ‘windless’ (νη- ‘not’ + ἄνεμος). αἰθήρ is the bright upper air; the literal layer keeps ‘aether’.

sentences.t:
ἔκ τ’ ἔφανεν πᾶσαι σκοπιαὶ καὶ πρώονες ἄκροι
καὶ νάπαι·
sentences.l:
and show forth all the lookout-peaks and the headlands, the high ones,
and the dells;
sentences.i: and all the lookout peaks and high headlands and dells come into view;
sentences.n: ἔκ τ’ … ἔφανεν is the epic third-person plural (for ἐφάνησαν) with its preverb apart (tmesis), ‘shone forth’; the aorist states what always happens in such a night, so the English puts it in the present. σκοπιαί are peaks from which one looks out, πρώονες jutting headlands (ἄκροι ‘high’), and νάπαι wooded dells. The unit ends mid-line, at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
οὐρανόθεν δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπερράγη ἄσπετος αἰθήρ,
πάντα δὲ εἴδεται ἄστρα, γέγηθε δέ τε φρένα ποιμήν·
sentences.l:
and from heaven bursts open the boundless aether,
and all the stars are seen, and glad in his wits is the shepherd;
sentences.i: and from heaven the boundless upper air bursts open, and all the stars are seen, and the shepherd is glad in his mind;
sentences.n: οὐρανόθεν is ‘from heaven’ (-θεν is a suffix of origin). ὑπερράγη is the aorist of a compound of ῥήγνυμι ‘break’, here ‘burst open’, again a general statement put in the present. ἄσπετος is ‘boundless’. εἴδεται is ‘is seen’, and γέγηθε the perfect of γηθέω, ‘is glad’; φρένα, an accusative of respect, is ‘in his wits’, the shepherd’s inner self; the English says ‘mind’. The unit begins in the middle of 8.558, after the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
τόσσα μεσηγὺ νεῶν ἠδὲ Ξάνθοιο ῥοάων
Τρώων καιόντων πυρὰ φαίνετο Ἰλιόθι πρό.
sentences.l:
So many between the ships and the streams of Xanthus
the Trojans burning, the fires shone before Ilios.
sentences.i: So many were the fires that the Trojans burned between the ships and the streams of Xanthus, shining before Ilios.
sentences.n: The simile’s second half. τόσσα … πυρά is ‘so many fires’, the second term of the comparison. μεσηγύ is ‘between’, and Ξάνθοιο ῥοάων ‘the streams of Xanthus’, the river. Τρώων καιόντων is a genitive absolute, ‘the Trojans burning (them)’, and πυρὰ φαίνετο ‘the fires shone’, with the singular verb after a neuter plural. Ἰλιόθι is ‘at Ilios’, with πρό ‘in front of’ (-θι is a suffix of place).

sentences.t:
χίλι’ ἄρ’ ἐν πεδίῳ πυρὰ καίετο, πὰρ δὲ ἑκάστῳ
εἴατο πεντήκοντα σέλᾳ πυρὸς αἰθομένοιο.
sentences.l:
A thousand fires then in the plain were burning, and beside each
sat fifty in the blaze of blazing fire.
sentences.i: A thousand fires, then, were burning in the plain, and beside each sat fifty men in the blaze of a blazing fire.
sentences.n: χίλι’ is ‘a thousand’ (χίλια, elided), and ἄρ’ is ‘so, then’. καίετο and εἴατο are the verbs of 554, now with a thousand fires. πὰρ δὲ ἑκάστῳ is ‘and beside each’ (πάρ = παρά), and πεντήκοντα ‘fifty’, which the Greek leaves without a noun; the English supplies ‘men’. σέλᾳ is the dative of σέλας ‘blaze’, and αἰθομένοιο the genitive participle of αἴθομαι ‘blaze’.

sentences.t:
ἵπποι δὲ κρῖ λευκὸν ἐρεπτόμενοι καὶ ὀλύρας
ἑσταότες παρ’ ὄχεσφιν ἐΰθρονον Ἠῶ μίμνον.
sentences.l:
And the horses, white barley feeding on and spelt,
standing beside the chariots, for fair-throned Dawn were waiting.
sentences.i: And the horses, feeding on white barley and spelt, stood beside the chariots and waited for fair-throned Dawn.
sentences.n: κρῖ is ‘barley’ (an indeclinable neuter, a shortened form of κριθή), and ὀλύρας ‘spelt’, a kind of grain; which grain exactly is not certain. ἐρεπτόμενοι is ‘feeding on’, and ἑσταότες the perfect participle of ἵστημι, ‘standing’; παρ’ ὄχεσφιν is ‘beside the chariots’ (-φιν is an old ending). ἐΰθρονον Ἠῶ is ‘fair-throned Dawn’, the Odyssey’s house rendering (ἐΰ- ‘fair’); the sense of -θρονος as ‘throne’ is the usual explanation, and some ancient readers took θρόνα as ‘flowers’, so it is not certain. μίμνον is ‘were waiting for’. The part ends with the horses waiting for the morning on which Hector has said the fight will be renewed.
